title: The Afternoon Brief: Senate Funds Government Through December 11
dek: The Senate cleared a bipartisan funding bill through December 11 while a wildfire in British Columbia forced more than 20,000 evacuations and a school shooting near Bangkok killed at least eight.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The Senate passed a continuing resolution funding the government through December 11 on a 90-6 vote, but the bill's fate now depends on the House, which passed a different, Democrat-opposed version before recess.
bottom_line: The Senate passed a bipartisan continuing resolution 90-6 on Saturday, funding the government through December 11, but the bill's path now runs through a House that passed a different, Democrat-opposed measure before recess. Separately, a wildfire in British Columbia forced more than 20,000 evacuations after doubling in size since Friday, and a school shooting near Bangkok killed at least eight people, including five school staff. The reporting does not tie these events together, and each carries its own open questions: the House's next move on funding, the wildfire's cause and containment, and how a 14-year-old obtained the firearm used in Thailand. Watch for the House's decision on which funding bill to advance, further evacuation and containment updates from British Columbia, and any official findings from Thai authorities on the shooting.
body: The day's most concrete development is fiscal: the Senate voted 90-6 on Saturday to approve a continuing resolution that would fund the federal government through December 11, clearing a chamber that needed 60 votes to act. Alongside that, two unrelated emergencies unfolded far from Washington: a wildfire in British Columbia forced more than 20,000 people to evacuate, and a school shooting near Bangkok killed at least eight people.

In Washington, the Senate's bipartisan continuing resolution keeps government funding at current levels, with some exceptions, through December 11. The bill now goes to the House, which passed a separate, GOP-led measure before its August recess that Democrats opposed. As the desk reported, the two chambers' bills differ, and it will fall to the House to decide how to reconcile them or take up the Senate's version.

In British Columbia, the Bald Range wildfire more than doubled in size since Friday, growing to over 36 square miles across the Summerland and Okanagan-Similkameen districts. Summerland's entire population of roughly 12,000 was ordered to evacuate, along with about 8,000 residents of neighboring Peachland. Power was lost across Summerland early Saturday, and the fire remained out of control as of Saturday morning.

Near Bangkok, a 14-year-old opened fire at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Nonthaburi province on Friday morning, killing at least eight people, including five school staff and his two grandparents, whom he is reported to have killed earlier that morning at the family home. A 12-year-old girl who was critically wounded died later in the hospital. Twenty-three others were wounded. The shooter took his own life after the attack.

The reporting does not connect these three events causally, and none of the inputs suggest a shared driver behind them. On the Senate bill, the reporting attributes the bipartisan approach to the practical need to reach the 60-vote threshold required to advance most legislation, a structural feature of the chamber rather than any single negotiation detail. On the wildfire, the reporting does not yet state a cause; officials have not indicated whether the growth reflects unusual conditions or familiar regional fire behavior. On the shooting, the reporting does not explain how the 14-year-old obtained the firearm or what oversight, if any, governs firearms in homes with minors in Thailand.
Desk boards were unavailable this cycle, so the record section is omitted for today's edition.

In the coming days, watch for the House's handling of the continuing resolution: whether Speaker Johnson brings up the Senate's bipartisan version, keeps pushing the chamber's own GOP-led measure, or seeks some blend of the two, with the government funding a fiscal cliff at stake if no bill reaches the president's desk. In British Columbia, watch for containment updates, any reports of structure loss, and whether Peachland and Summerland residents receive timelines for returning home. Near Bangkok, watch for any official findings on how the shooter obtained the weapon and whether Thai authorities discuss firearm storage or oversight rules in response.
